newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-MALDINI LAUNCHES "OPERATION NICENESS" IN PALERMO.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-MALDINI LAUNCHES "OPERATION NICENESS" IN PALERMO.

text.p: When Cesare Maldini chose Palermo as the venue for his debut as Italy manager, winning Wednesday's friendly with Northern Ireland was maybe not foremost in his mind.
Afterall, as a player, Maldini was on the losing side when he made his professional debut on the same ground with Trieste in 1953.
But results aside, the Sicilian capital represents the perfect place for the national coach to start winning back the hearts and minds of a soccer-mad nation.
"I chose Palermo because I can still remember the warmth of the reception given my Under-21 team," Maldini said.
Under Maldini's predecessor Arrigo Sacchi, the popularity of the national team plummeted after first round elimination from Euro 96 and a humiliating defeat to Bosnia.
Empty seats at Perugia last October for Italy's World Cup qualifier with Giorgia, and consistently high TV ratings for his Under-21 team paved the way for Maldini's promotion.
Now, the new manager must heal the rift between the azzurri and the public.
"Operazione Simpatia (operation niceness) has already started," hailed sports daily Gazzetta dello Sport.
"Once there was a national team that left for the match on board a private charter flight," wrote the editorial, "Maldini's squad took a normal flight among the people."

However, not even Maldini's popularity would survive elimination from the 1998 World Cup and the match with Northern Ireland is his only warm-up for the vital Wembley qualifying clash against England next month.
England manager Glenn Hoddle is also due to fly to Palermo to spy on his rival's team.
Maldini has acknowledged Northern Ireland were consciously chosen as a test for the England match. "We have to arm ourselves for the aerial game," he said.
Ironically, Maldini's 'new' side looks like Sacchi's old team -- and Sacchi, now the Milan manager, even gets the blame for that.
"I'm sorry but in five years Arrigo called up 93 (players). I'd have had to look at serie B to come up with something new," Maldini said in a barely concealed slight at his predecessor.
Maldini's team might resemble Sacchi's on paper but, on the pitch, the veteran manager represents a return to Italy's past.
Assistent to Enzo Bearzot during Italy's 1982 World Cup triumph, Maldini will experiment with the five-man sweeper system that once anchored all Italian national teams.
With Franco Baresi retired from international football, the libero role will fall to his Milan teammate Alessandro Costacurta or Juventus's Ciro Ferrara.
Maldini's son Paolo will stay at left-back and will keep the captain's armband.
Also unlike Sacchi, often a prisoner of his own schemes, Maldini will adapt tactics to teams. "We are not the strongest team in the world," he said on Monday.
It is unlikely that Maldini will have to adapt much to face an injury-hit Northern Ireland team that has never won in Italy.

Bryan Hamilton's side, missing Newcastle midfielder Keith Gillespie and Leicester's Neil Lennon, includes just three premier league players - Stephen Morrow of Arsenal and West Ham's Keith Rowland and Michael Hughes.
John McCarthy of first division Port Vale flew to Palermo on Tuesday as a late replacement to bolster a team that recently held Germany to a draw in a World Cup qualifying match.
"I am sure we will give them a good test," said Hamilton, "and I hope Glenn will learn something from it."
Teams:
Italy - Angelo Peruzzi, Paolo Maldini, Alessandro Costacurta, Amedeo Carboni, Ciro Ferrara, Angelo Di Livio, Roberto Di Matteo, Demetrio Albertini, Dino Baggio, Gianfranco Zola, Pierluigi Casiraghi.

Northern Ireland (from) - Alan Fettis, Tommy Wright, Michael Hughes, Keith Rowland, Stephen Lomas, Mark Graham, Gerry Taggart, Barry Hunger, Kevin Horlock, Stephen Morrow, James Quinn, George O'Boyle, Danny Griffin, Jeff Whitley, Anton Rogan, Robbie Dennison, Phil Mulryne, Nigel Worthington, John McCarthy
